#!/bin/bash

# Flux batch script converted from LSF
# Note: Flux does not support in-script directives for resource specification
# This script should be submitted with the following command:
# flux batch -N 600 -n 3600 -t 10m --job-name=COLOR --output=color-3600g.o{{id}} script.sh
#
# Resource specifications:
# -N 600       : 600 nodes (from -nnodes 600)
# -n 3600      : 3600 tasks (from jsrun -n3600)
# -t 10m       : 10 minute walltime (from -W 10)
# --job-name=COLOR : job name (from -J COLOR)
# --output=color-3600g.o{{id}} : output file with job ID (from -o color-3600g.o%J)
#
# Note: Flux uses {{id}} or {{jobid}} for job ID instead of %J

# Original LSF project/account: CSC275MCCLURE
# LSF: -P CSC275MCCLURE
# Note: Flux uses banks/accounts through flux-accounting
# Set at submission if flux-accounting is configured:
# flux batch --setattr=bank=CSC275MCCLURE ...
# Performance impact: Without bank specification, job runs under default account
# which could affect priority, resource limits, or accounting tracking

# Job feature/environment: NVME
# LSF: #BSUB -env "all,JOB_FEATURE=NVME" (commented out in original)
# Note: LSF job features specify node properties or requirements
# Flux handles node properties through resource constraints
# This was commented out in the original, so not translating
# If NVME storage is required, consult site-specific Flux configuration:
# - May use --requires or --setattr for node properties
# - Example: --requires="nvme" (if configured in Flux resource graph)
# Performance impact: Job may not get nodes with NVME if not specified

# Walltime: 10 minutes
# LSF: -W 10 (10 minutes)
# Flux: -t 10m or -t 600s
# Note: Flux time format: #m (minutes), #h (hours), #s (seconds), #d (days)

# Output file:
# LSF: -o color-3600g.o%J (where %J is job ID)
# Flux: --output=color-3600g.o{{id}} (where {{id}} is job ID)
# Note: Flux uses {{id}}, {{jobid}}, or {{name}} for substitutions

date

# Module environment
module load gcc cuda

# LSF Spectrum MPI environment setup (commented out in original)
#source $OLCF_SPECTRUM_MPI_ROOT/jsm_pmix/bin/export_smpi_env -gpu
# Note: This is LSF/Summit-specific MPI setup
# Flux uses different MPI integration (typically PMI/PMIx)
# Ensure MPI library is built with Flux PMI support

# Working directory setup (commented out in original)
#cd /ccs/home/mcclurej/summit/build/ScaLBL/example/Sph1896/
#cp Domain.in.8g Domain.in

# Environment variable
export LBPM_WIA_DIR=$HOME/summit/build/LBPM-WIA/tests

# Change to working directory
cd /gpfs/alpinetds/csc275/scratch/mcclurej/SCALING/WEAK/3600p

# LSF jsrun command conversion to Flux
# Original: jsrun -n3600 -r6 -g1 -c1 -brs --smpiargs="-gpu" $LBPM_WIA_DIR/TestCommD3Q19
#
# jsrun parameters:
# -n3600: 3600 resource sets (total MPI tasks)
# -r6: 6 resource sets per node (600 nodes × 6 = 3600 tasks)
# -g1: 1 GPU per resource set
# -c1: 1 CPU per resource set
# -brs: bind resources to resource set
# --smpiargs="-gpu": Spectrum MPI arguments for GPU support
#
# Flux equivalent:
# flux run -N 600 -n 3600 -g 1 -c 1 [--setattr options for binding]
#
# Note: jsrun's resource set model doesn't directly map to Flux
# Flux parameters:
# -N 600: distribute across 600 nodes (matching -r6 with 600 nodes)
# -n 3600: 3600 total tasks
# -g 1: 1 GPU per task (note: this may allocate 3600 GPUs total)
# -c 1: 1 core per task
#
# GPU allocation clarification:
# Original: 600 nodes with 6 tasks/node, 1 GPU per task = 3600 GPUs total
# Summit nodes have 6 GPUs each, so this allocates all GPUs
# Flux: -g 1 means 1 GPU per task
# With -n 3600, this requests 3600 GPUs total
# Alternative: -g 3600 (total GPUs) but this is not standard Flux syntax
# Verify GPU allocation with your Flux configuration

flux run -N 600 -n 3600 -c 1 -g 1 $LBPM_WIA_DIR/TestCommD3Q19

# Note on jsrun translation:
# 1. Resource binding (-brs): Flux uses different binding mechanisms
#    Consider: --setattr=system.shell.options.cpu-affinity=per-task
#    Or: -o cpu-affinity=per-task (if supported)
#    Consult Flux documentation for hwloc-based binding
#
# 2. Spectrum MPI GPU support (--smpiargs="-gpu"):
#    Flux uses different MPI implementation (not Spectrum MPI)
#    GPU support depends on MPI library and Flux integration
#    Ensure MPI library supports GPU-aware communication
#    May need CUDA-aware MPI (OpenMPI, MPICH with CUDA support)
#
# 3. Resource set model:
#    jsrun's resource sets group tasks, cores, and GPUs
#    Flux allocates resources per task
#    Verify task-to-GPU mapping matches application expectations

exit

# Complete submission command with all options:
# flux batch -N 600 -n 3600 -c 1 -g 1 -t 10m \
#   --job-name=COLOR \
#   --output=color-3600g.o{{id}} \
#   --setattr=bank=CSC275MCCLURE \
#   script.sh
#
# Note: Adjust GPU allocation based on actual requirements:
# - If 1 GPU per task is correct: -g 1 (3600 GPUs total)
# - If 1 GPU per node is needed: use different approach
# - Verify with 'flux resource list' before submission

reasons: GPU resource allocation conflict: The submission command specifies 'flux batch -N 600 -n 3600' but the flux run command inside the script also specifies '-N 600 -n 3600 -g 1', which is redundant and potentially problematic. The batch allocation already reserves resources, and flux run within the batch should use those allocated resources.

GPU allocation ambiguity: With '-g 1' per task and '-n 3600' tasks, this requests 3600 GPUs total. However, the batch submission command does not include any GPU allocation ('-g' flag), creating a mismatch between requested and allocated resources. The batch command should include '-g 3600' or the appropriate GPU specification.

Resource specification mismatch: The documented batch submission command 'flux batch -N 600 -n 3600 -t 10m --job-name=COLOR --output=color-3600g.o{{id}} script.sh' does not include cores-per-task specification, but the flux run command uses '-c 1'. This should be specified at batch submission time for proper resource allocation.

Missing memory specification: Neither the batch submission nor the flux run command specifies memory requirements. For a large-scale job with 3600 tasks, explicit memory allocation is critical to avoid resource contention or OOM errors.
issues: The flux run command should not re-specify node count (-N) and task count (-n) when running inside a batch allocation. It should either use all allocated resources by default or specify a subset. The current specification '-N 600 -n 3600' is redundant with the batch allocation.

The complete submission command at the bottom includes '-c 1' in the batch command ('flux batch -N 600 -n 3600 -c 1 -g 1 -t 10m'), but the primary documented command at the top does not. This creates confusion about the correct submission syntax.

The GPU allocation strategy is unclear. If the goal is 1 GPU per task (6 GPUs per node × 600 nodes = 3600 GPUs), the batch submission should explicitly request: 'flux batch -N 600 -n 3600 -c 1 -g 3600 -t 10m' or use a per-task GPU specification if Flux supports it.

The output file placeholder uses '{{id}}' which should be verified. Flux may use '{{id}}', '{{jobid}}', or '{id}' (single braces) depending on version. This should be tested with the specific Flux installation.
The bank/account specification '--setattr=bank=CSC275MCCLURE' is only shown in the complete submission command but not in the primary documented command, creating inconsistency.

The flux run command inside a batch script should typically be simplified to just specify the application command, letting it inherit the batch allocation: 'flux run $LBPM_WIA_DIR/TestCommD3Q19' or use explicit resource distribution if needed: 'flux run -n 3600 -c 1 -g 1 $LBPM_WIA_DIR/TestCommD3Q19'
The 10-minute walltime may be insufficient for a large-scale job with 3600 tasks. Consider if this is adequate for initialization, execution, and cleanup.
No validation that the working directory '/gpfs/alpinetds/csc275/scratch/mcclurej/SCALING/WEAK/3600p' exists or is accessible before cd command.
The conversion notes mention resource binding (-brs from jsrun) but no binding options are implemented in the flux run command. This may affect performance on NUMA systems.
